engine.name: A.R.I.A. Aging Engine
engine.purpose: Evaluate how unresolved operational work changes in significance as time passes. The engine prevents legitimate lower-priority work from remaining indefinitely buried while ensuring age alone does not manufacture false urgency or override actual consequence.
principles: Age is operational evidence, not automatic urgency.
Legitimate work should not remain permanently buried because newer urgent work continually arrives.
Old low-value work must not automatically become more important than newer high-consequence work.
Aging should consider why work remains unresolved.
Waiting, delegated, blocked, snoozed, and actively progressing work age differently.
Time sensitivity and age are related but not identical.
Repeated deferral may be more meaningful than elapsed time alone.
Aging may justify priority reevaluation but does not own canonical priority.
Aging may justify renewed attention but does not own user-facing attention.
Resolved work does not continue accumulating operational age.

applicable_conditions: work item has existed across multiple evaluation cycles
work item has been repeatedly deferred
work item has received insufficient attention relative to its operational significance

fresh.description: The work is sufficiently new that elapsed age adds little or no additional operational significance.

normal.description: The work remains within a reasonable unresolved period given its context.

maturing.description: Elapsed time or repeated deferral is becoming operationally relevant and should influence reevaluation.

stale.description: The work has remained unresolved long enough that its current state, ownership, need, or priority should be actively reassessed.

chronic.description: The work has persisted through repeated opportunities for resolution or reassessment and requires explicit disposition.

paused.description: Operational aging is intentionally limited because a supported future condition or authorized pause explains the lack of progress.

resolved.description: The underlying work has reached a terminal state and no longer accumulates active operational age.

unresolved.description: Available information is insufficient to determine the appropriate aging state.

rules: Calendar age and operational inactivity must remain distinguishable.
Meaningful progress may reduce staleness without resetting the historical age of the work item.
Administrative edits must not falsely reset meaningful inactivity.
A status change without substantive operational change must not automatically reset aging.
The most relevant aging reference depends on the current state of the work.
Missing timestamps must remain unknown rather than invented.

active: Unresolved actionable work should accumulate aging significance when it repeatedly loses attention to other work.
Meaningful execution progress may reduce the need for aging escalation.
waiting: Waiting time should be evaluated against the expected response or condition when one exists.
Waiting within a reasonable supported response window should not create artificial aging pressure.
Waiting beyond reasonable expectations may increase aging significance.
delegated: Healthy delegated work should not age merely because the user is not personally touching it.
Delegated work may become stale when expected progress, completion, or acknowledgement repeatedly fails to materialize.
blocked: Blocked work should not become artificially urgent when no useful intervention exists.
Long-lived blockers should still trigger reassessment of alternate paths, ownership, scope, or continuing need.
snoozed: An authorized snooze suppresses attention until its trigger or expiration.
Snoozing does not erase historical age.
Repeated snoozing may itself become an aging signal.
in_progress: Work making meaningful progress should not be treated as stale solely because its total duration is long.
Progress should be evaluated relative to the nature and expected duration of the work.

signals: action repeatedly acknowledged but not performed
work repeatedly moved to a later planning period
rules: Repeated deferral may increase operational significance even when calendar age is modest.
Deferral caused by valid dependencies should remain distinguishable from discretionary postponement.
A.R.I.A. should not interpret every scheduling change as avoidance.
Repeated discretionary deferral should eventually force explicit reconsideration of priority, ownership, scope, or continued need.
The system should not permit indefinite deferral without periodic disposition.

levels.none: Age currently adds no meaningful pressure.
levels.low: Age should be considered during ordinary reevaluation.
levels.moderate: Age or deferral now materially supports priority or attention reassessment.
levels.high: The work requires explicit disposition because continued unresolved status is becoming operationally unacceptable.

rules: Aging pressure must not be derived from elapsed time alone.
Consequential unresolved work may accumulate pressure faster than trivial work.
Strategic work may accumulate meaningful aging pressure even without a hard deadline.
Work with no continuing value should be considered for legitimate resolution rather than artificial priority escalation.
High aging pressure requires explicit reassessment, not automatic maximum priority.

anti_starvation.purpose: Prevent valid lower-priority work from being permanently displaced by an endless stream of newer urgent work.
rules: The engine should detect work that remains valid but repeatedly receives no execution opportunity.
Repeated displacement should increase the strength of the recommendation for Priority Engine reevaluation.
Anti-starvation behavior must preserve consequence-based prioritization.
Low-priority work should not leapfrog critical work solely because it is older.
Protected execution time may be recommended for strategically valuable or chronically displaced work.
Attention Engine determines whether and when anti-starvation recommendations should be surfaced.

questions: Is the original outcome still relevant?
Does the current owner remain correct?
Is the work actually waiting rather than actionable?
Should the scope be reduced or separated?
Has completion occurred without being recognized?
Has the work become more consequential because of delay?

rules: Strategically important work may have low immediate urgency while still suffering from repeated displacement.
Lack of an external deadline must not make strategic work invisible.
Strategic value may justify protected attention before the work becomes urgent.
Aging may strengthen the case for protected execution time when strategic work remains repeatedly displaced.
Priority Engine remains responsible for canonical priority evaluation.
Aging Engine provides aging and starvation signals to Priority Engine.
Priority Engine owns canonical priority scoring and banding.
Age may influence priority but must not independently overwrite it.
Aging must not automatically increment a priority number on a fixed schedule.
Priority changes must remain consequence-aware.
Aging Engine may identify work that deserves renewed consideration.
Attention Engine determines whether and how the user should see it.
A stale item does not automatically justify interruption.
Chronic strategically important work may justify protected attention rather than emergency interruption.
Follow-Up Engine governs pursuit and verification timing.
Repeatedly missed or rescheduled follow-ups may contribute to aging pressure.
Aging must not independently send or schedule follow-up communication.
Dependency Engine determines whether unresolved conditions block progress.
Aging Engine evaluates the significance of long-lived dependency states.
A blocked item should not become falsely urgent merely because the blocker is old.
Long-lived blockers should trigger reassessment of alternatives and continuing relevance.
Delegation Engine governs delegated execution.
Healthy delegation should not be penalized by user inactivity.
Repeated failed expectations or unexplained lack of progress may increase aging pressure.
Commitment Engine governs promises and commitment state.
Approaching or missed commitments may accelerate aging significance.
Aging must not redefine the terms of a commitment.
Resolution Engine determines whether work has legitimately reached a terminal state.
Stale or chronic work should be explicitly reviewed for legitimate resolution.
Age alone is never sufficient reason to close work.
Terminally resolved work stops accumulating active aging pressure.
Aging reevaluation must preserve historical age and deferral history.
Reevaluation should distinguish legitimate waiting from neglect.
Reevaluation should determine whether the work remains operationally relevant.
Material aging changes may trigger Priority, Attention, Follow-Up, Dependency, Delegation, Commitment, or Resolution reevaluation.

requirements: Aging output must reference the applicable work_item_id.
Aging must preserve the distinction between calendar age and meaningful inactivity.
Derived aging pressure must remain explainable.
Aging must not directly overwrite canonical priority.
Material aging changes must be available to dependent operational engines.

guardrails: Do not make work urgent solely because it is old.
Do not allow legitimate work to remain buried indefinitely.
Do not automatically increment priority on a timer.
Do not reset meaningful age because of administrative edits.
Do not erase historical age when work is snoozed.
Do not treat every reschedule as avoidance.
Do not repeatedly surface blocked work when no useful intervention exists.
Do not close work merely because it became stale.
Do not preserve obsolete work merely because it has existed a long time.
Do not bypass the Attention Engine for user-facing presentation.
Do not bypass the Resolution Engine for terminal disposition.
Do not modify Core reasoning architecture as part of aging management.
